sources.title: How apps hit 300M+ views a month: Content Rewards clipper playbook
sources.originalTitle: how to get 300 million views for your app in 30 days
sources.summary: Alex, CMO of Content Rewards, lays out the playbook apps use to reach hundreds of millions of views a month through paid clippers and UGC creators. It covers building a clippable aha moment into the product, finding simple viral formats, writing the brief like a course, and training and rewarding creators. It also promotes his own platform.

principles.text: Build a clippable aha moment into the product: the user does something and the app produces a shareable result.
principles.quote: have a moment in your app that showcases a result that's easily clippable. that's the thing that will make you go viral.

principles.text: Test virality by asking how likely people are to pay to learn the result. That predicts the app's success.
principles.quote: "how likely are people to pay to know this result/get this outcome" and that's your answer to how successful your app will be.

principles.text: Simple, low-effort content converts better because it blends into the feed. It also lets more clippers join.
principles.quote: simple content looks less ad-like, and it's easier to convert cuz it blends in with the algorithm better, so people think it's a natural recommendation.

principles.text: Write the creator brief as a full course, not a requirements list, if you want consistent content at mass scale.
principles.quote: you need to create a content brief that is practically a course on how to create content for your app software. not just a requirement list, nobody follows that at mass scale.

principles.text: Build a no-download web version of the app so creators can generate the aha moment instantly.
principles.quote: creators shouldn't need to download your app, create an account, or do any of that to make content about it.

principles.text: Add milestone bonuses on top of CPM pay. They motivate creators more than passive payouts.
principles.quote: Sometimes creators will grind harder for the $100 milestone bonus than the passive CPM, because milestones just feel like something they can target and win.

sources.title: How an app scaled to $300k MRR with 596M views via a clipper/creator network
sources.originalTitle: how we scaled an app to 300k/mrr in just 2 months w/ 596m views
sources.summary: Alex breaks down a Content Rewards case study: an app went from low-five-figure to $300k MRR in two months on about $163k of creator payouts. The playbook is proven viral formats, a full creator operating system, and a per-post payout cap that makes viral outliers nearly free.

principles.text: Find proven viral formats yourself before scaling; the research is what makes the scale work.
principles.quote: they spent a month finding what worked. the research is what makes the scale work.

principles.text: Make content people watch for itself, with the app as the payoff, never the whole video, so it doesn't read as an ad.
principles.quote: the content is the hook. the product is the payoff. if your app is the entire video, nobody watches.

principles.text: Cap payouts per post so every clip beyond the cap is free reach and blended CPM falls as campaigns grow.
principles.quote: set your max payout at a level that motivates creators; and know that every clip that blows past the cap threshold is essentially free reach.

principles.text: Treat creator onboarding like a product: agreement, modules, weekly content bank, not just a brief.
principles.quote: the brands that win treat creator onboarding like a product; content banks, warm-up playbooks, confidentiality agreements, bonus incentive layers.

principles.text: Layer a second incentive tied to installs on top of CPM so you drive both reach and conversion.
principles.quote: they layered a leaderboard that rewarded top creators based on actual app downloads via link-in-bio.

principles.text: Run Instagram, TikTok and YouTube at once to compound reach and learn where the format performs best.
principles.quote: running all three simultaneously gives you compounding reach from one campaign budget and tells you fast where your format performs best.

sources.title: How a Content Rewards app hit $200k MRR and 651M views in 3 months at a $0.27 effective CPM
sources.originalTitle: How this app scaled to $200k MRR in 3 months w/ 651m views
sources.summary: Alex's case study of an app that scaled to $200k MRR with 651M views and $173K in creator payouts using seven clipping campaigns. Covers finding a format first, running parallel campaigns, writing briefs that hook viewers, using payout caps for free reach, and building a small dedicated creator base.

principles.text: Find a winning content format before you spend to scale it; clippers amplify what already works.
principles.quote: if you want your campaign to go crazy you need to give your clippers an idea of what formats will do well and what won't

principles.text: Run several campaigns in parallel with different rates, caps and formats so you learn what works in weeks, not months.
principles.quote: because they ran and experimented with different things, they found out which formats worked in weeks instead of months

principles.text: Brief creators to lead with something interesting and mention the product at the end; it lifted approval and halved CPM.
principles.quote: a video that talks about something interesting first pulls the viewer in and makes them watch till the end

principles.text: A small group of serious creators beats a big group of casual ones.
principles.quote: a small group of serious creators is SO much better than a big group of less serious ones

principles.text: Build loyal creators yourself via a thorough course, regular live calls, and 1-1 mentoring through hired mentors.
principles.quote: make a very thorough course. guide your creators from A-Z, teach them EVERYTHING you can about clipping and what works for your product in general

principles.text: Set a sensible payout cap: views past the cap are free reach, driving effective CPM far below paid ads.
principles.quote: every view you get after the cap is free reach, if you can set a decent cap you will generate a very good ROI

sources.title: How to reach $10k/mo in 90 days from zero by clipping: Alex's day-by-day plan
sources.originalTitle: if i lost everything tomorrow, here's exactly how i'd make $10k/mo in 90 days with nothing
sources.summary: Alex lays out a 90-day plan to go from nothing to $10k+/mo as a content clipper, who reposts brand footage for pay per view. It covers niche and campaign selection, dedicated accounts, a daily batch editing workflow built around hooks, how earnings compound with account history, and hiring editors for leverage.

principles.text: Brands are shifting budget from paid ads to paying creators for organic-looking posts, which is far cheaper per view.
principles.quote: instead of paying meta $10 to show people ads they skip, they can pay regular people to post organic-looking content about their product from their own accounts for $0.30 CPM

principles.text: Short-form algorithms reward watch time, not follower count, so a zero-follower account can still get distribution.
principles.quote: a 0-follower account can generate hundreds of thousands of views b/c short-form algorithms don't care who you are. they care whether people watch past the first 3 seconds

principles.text: Pick campaigns where you have genuine interest and skill; a lower-CPM niche you're good at can beat a higher-CPM one you're not.
principles.quote: i know people absolutely PRINTING with the lower CPM campaigns

principles.text: Use one dedicated account per niche so the algorithm builds a clean audience graph and knows who to show your content to.
principles.quote: dedicated accounts = clean signal = better distribution from day 1

principles.text: Write hooks before editing and reuse the clip body: hook variations drive most performance and each extra variant takes only minutes.
principles.quote: i write 5 different hooks per campaign in my notes app before i touch the editor. this is the most important 15 minutes of my day b/c the hook determines 90% of a clip's performance

principles.text: Expect an ugly first week; the early goal is building editing reps and consistent posting, not money, and most people quit too soon.
principles.quote: the people who fail at this model almost always fail here. they judge the entire thing based on 7 days of data and walk away.

sources.title: Content arbitrage: how Alex says creators earn by reposting brand clips at scale
sources.originalTitle: how to get obscenely rich posting the same videos over and over again
sources.summary: Alex pitches "content arbitrage": brands pay everyday people to clip and repost their footage on TikTok, Reels and Shorts because many organic posts look like a cultural moment rather than an ad. He gives income tiers, the three levers separating top earners (volume, niche, hooks), and urges joining early. It is also a promotion for his employer's platform, so the income claims are unverified.

principles.text: Many organic-looking posts at once read to the algorithm as a cultural moment, not an ad campaign, so brands pay everyday accounts to post.
principles.quote:
if 500 regular accounts post organic-looking content about their product at the same time, the algorithm doesn't see an ad campaign

it sees a cultural moment

principles.text: Re-editing the same footage per account makes each version a distinct signal, so one core message reaches many separate audience pools.
principles.quote: every time you re-edit a video, even slightly, the platform registers it as a completely unique piece of content

principles.text: Top earners run a repeatable batch process (batch-edit and schedule) instead of posting when inspired.
principles.quote: they batch-edit 20-30 clips on a sunday, schedule them across the week, and let the system run.

principles.text: Pick a few high-CPM verticals and go deep rather than spreading across everything.
principles.quote: the highest earners pick 2-3 high-CPM verticals and go deep instead of spreading thin across everything

principles.text: The hook (first 1-2 seconds) decides performance, so test many hooks on the same clip.
principles.quote: the raw footage might be identical. but the hook, the first 1-2 seconds, determines everything

principles.text: Removing friction (invoicing, negotiation, payouts) is what moved this model from niche to mainstream; the barrier was never skill.
principles.quote: the barrier that used to filter people out was never skill. it was friction

sources.originalTitle: how to beat companies spending $30M/year on ads (with your iphone)
sources.summary: Alex argues paid ads are structurally losing to volume-based organic creator distribution. Brands give raw footage and blueprints to hundreds or thousands of ordinary creators who post native-looking clips, which the algorithm treats as a trend. Includes his claimed CTR/CPM numbers and how the skill compounds. Note: promotes his own platform, Content Rewards, and the figures are self-reported.

principles.text: People distrust branded ads but treat regular people's posts like peer recommendations, so organic creator clips outperform paid ads.
principles.quote: people fundamentally do not trust branded content anymore

principles.text: Win with volume: hundreds of imperfect clips beat one perfect ad, because many accounts posting at once reads to the algorithm as a trend.
principles.quote: not one perfect ad seen by millions. hundreds of imperfect clips seen by millions

principles.text: Distribute the marketing budget across many creators instead of paying a platform; you ride the algorithm rather than fight it.
principles.quote: the company spending $10M on ads is fighting the algorithm

principles.text: Short-form algorithms distribute on early engagement and hook quality, not follower count or production value, so the entry barrier is low.
principles.quote: a brand new account w/ 0 followers can outperform a branded 100k follower account if the opening 3 seconds are better

principles.text: Give creators raw assets, talking points and a campaign blueprint so they only need to repackage with a strong hook and native pacing.
principles.quote: the brand provides the raw content. the talking points. the campaign blueprint

principles.text: Skills compound with volume: editing speed, hook instinct, algorithmic trust and platform trust all improve the longer you post consistently.
principles.quote: this is the single highest-leverage skill in marketing and it only comes from volume

sources.title: Netflix Sucks at Marketing: why a paid clipper program beats $89 CAC
sources.summary: Alex argues Netflix wastes $2.9B on marketing ($89 per subscriber) while suppressing its cheapest channel, user clips. Using Kick's clipping program as proof, he lays out a tiered CPM-paid clipper model that could cut CAC to $1.2-$4, and why incumbents won't adopt it.

principles.text: Clips are commercials that don't feel like commercials; the content itself is the marketing.
principles.quote: clips are commercials that don't feel like commercials.

principles.text: Pay creators per view (CPM) to distribute your content at scale; it's far cheaper than traditional ads.
principles.quote: Thirty billion views for six million dollars.

principles.text: Discovery happens on short-form platforms before someone subscribes, so in-product recommendation alone is a distribution gap.
principles.quote: Netflix's recommendation algorithm only works on people who are already subscribed.

principles.text: Don't punish fans who spread your content; takedowns kill organic discovery, your best free distribution.
principles.quote: The show loses all organic discovery. Viewership numbers disappoint. The show gets cancelled after one season.

principles.text: Structure creator programs in tiers: open entry at low CPM, verified partners at higher CPM, top performers with bonuses and revenue share.
principles.quote: Tier 1: Open program Anyone can join. $0.6 CPM payout.

principles.text: Stress-test the math: even if conversion is 10x too optimistic, the channel still wins on CAC.
principles.quote: Even if my conversion rate is 10x too optimistic, they're still acquiring subscribers at $12 instead of $89.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex, CMO of Content Rewards, lays out the playbook apps use to reach hundreds of millions of views a month through paid clippers and UGC creators. It covers building a clippable aha moment into the product, finding simple viral formats, writing the brief like a course, and training and rewarding creators. It also promotes his own platform.

chunks.heading: Build the app around a clippable "aha moment"
chunks.text:
Alex says every app that blew up through Content Rewards was built around virality. It had a moment that is easy to understand in a slideshow or screen recording: you do something, and the app produces a result.

- Examples he gives: Cal AI (photo of food, shows calories), a fishing app (photo of a catch, says it is "top 1% rarest fish"), a room app (photo of your room, designs a better layout).
- Test for success: ask "how likely are people to pay to know this result/get this outcome". That answer predicts how well the app will do.
- Lookmaxing apps went viral because rating people is controversial, and everyone wanted to know their own rating, which drove high conversion.
- Context he cites: one app that joined Content Rewards in February passed 830 million views by mid-June. It did close to 400 million views in a month, on about $250,000 total spend across all its campaigns. He has seen apps in different niches reach six-figure MRR in 2-3 months.

chunks.heading: Find viral formats, then keep the content simple
chunks.text:
Alex's process for finding formats (from a May 30 post he links): brainstorm about 50 niche keywords with ChatGPT, then log findings in a Notion table with tabs for link, sound, hook, format, visuals and editing notes.

Once a format is producing a couple of million views a month, he looks for scalability through clipping:
- The best-performing videos and slideshows look like they took 30 seconds to 5 minutes to make.
- Simple content looks less ad-like and blends into the algorithm, so it reads as a natural recommendation and converts better.
- Easy content means more clippers can post it, more clippers can be attracted, and there are more chances to go viral. "2 slide slideshows often have higher conversion rates than your 1-2 min long UGC video."
- He recommends hiring a few creators and clippers to test angles and find 10 to 20 easily replicable viral formats, then turning them into a content bank.

chunks.heading: Build the brief like a course
chunks.text:
Alex calls the brief the most important part of a campaign. To get thousands of videos with a consistent message, it must be "practically a course", not a requirements list ("nobody follows that at mass scale"). Components:
- **Content bank:** for each format, give a name, example posts, the music to use (viral songs tend to boost videos), context on what happens in the video or slides, caption ideas, and AI prompts if used. Give clippers as much as possible.
- **Content creation course:** Notion modules covering A to Z: campaign details, account setup (profile picture, bio), warming up the account, creating the content (with videos and all links), managing content to push the app, and submitting posts to the campaign. He says his template cuts setup time by 50%.
- **Do's and don'ts page:** examples of correct posts plus deliberately wrong ones (captions placed too high, wrong template or logo, wrong editing style).

chunks.heading: Add a creator contract and a no-install web version
chunks.text:
**Contract.** Most founders skip it. Draft it with ChatGPT, have creators sign it (e.g. on Tally) before posting, and put it at the top of the brief. Clauses he suggests:
- Right to reuse the content in ads later.
- A minimum time the content must stay up, with payment at risk if deleted earlier.
- CPM and max pay terms stated clearly.
- Account ownership if the account takes off.
- No working for competing apps.

It prevents disputes and legal headaches once content blows up.

**Influencer web version.** He calls this underrated: creators should not need to download the app or sign up. Build a web version where they enter their own inputs and get a customized output (screenshot, video, the aha moment) to overlay on their videos and slideshows. The goal is to make hundreds or thousands of versions of the aha moment easy to produce.

chunks.heading: Run the creator program: Discord, bonuses, and refreshing the machine
chunks.text:
**Two fulfillment routes on Content Rewards** (he is its CMO, so this is a promotion of his company; the platform claims over 2 million clippers and UGC creators):
- Agency route: verified agencies do outreach, find creators, manage the campaign, and can even write the brief.
- Self-fulfill: run everything yourself and recruit extra creators beyond those the platform brings.

**Train creators on Discord:**
- Bi-weekly calls to answer questions.
- Personalized tickets to coach individuals.
- A resources category.
- A top-performing category showing best videos and creators posting payouts.
- A leaderboard channel with the weekly top earner or view accumulator. Seeing others win motivates creators.

**Milestone bonuses on top of CPM.** Example: $100 for every 100 downloads from a creator's custom affiliate link. He says creators sometimes grind harder for a milestone than for passive CPM, because it feels like a target they can win. Design it so top creators always earn more and stay for months.

**Keep refreshing.** To sustain 300-400 million views a month, keep adding new angles, hooks and content bank entries, and keep helping creators find new formats. Repurposing proven formats in German, French and Spanish opens new markets, and they act as practically new formats.

chunks.heading: Economics: organic CPM campaigns vs ads
chunks.text:
Alex's pitch for the "new model" of organic campaigns:
- CPMs on Content Rewards can be as low as $0.16 to $0.30, with the highest usually $1 or less. He contrasts this with traditional CPMs of $20 to $30.
- A max payout cap limits cost on any single viral video to about $300 to $600, or whatever cap is set.
- You pay only for videos that actually generate views, not for influencer posts that do not convert.
- He says apps 10xed revenue in a month at a fraction of what ads would have cost.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex breaks down a Content Rewards case study: an app went from low-five-figure to $300k MRR in two months on about $163k of creator payouts. The playbook is proven viral formats, a full creator operating system, and a per-post payout cap that makes viral outliers nearly free.

chunks.heading: How Alex scaled an app to $300k MRR with 596M views on Content Rewards
chunks.text:
- **Result (Jan to May 2026):** An app that started at low-to-mid five figures MRR reached $300k+ MRR and about $700k in revenue.
- **Spend and reach:** $162,805 in creator payouts bought 596M views.
- **Volume:** The campaigns drew 38,882 submissions, of which 24,773 clips were approved.
- **Network:** Alex says Content Rewards has a network of 696k creators and clippers.
- **Comparison:** He says the same spend-to-revenue ratio "would be impossible with Meta or any other type of marketing."
- **Ongoing spend:** The brand's marketing spend was about $80-90k per month.
- **Process, not content:** "you don't need to copy their exact content. you need to copy their process."
- **Platform handling:** Content Rewards handles creator discovery, joining, submissions, view verification, content review and payments through Whop. The founders never touched an invoice or a spreadsheet.

chunks.heading: Find viral formats before scaling spend
chunks.text:
- The app was not starting from zero. It already had a product users loved.
- The founders found their own viral formats by testing with clippers, creators and influencers.
- That testing took them to 10-20k MRR organically.
- A viable format has three traits: proven viral, easy to replicate, easy to scale.
- Alex says they spent about a month on format research: "the research is what makes the scale work."
- His advice to brands is to test the formats yourself, or hire a creator or clipper on a retainer to find proven viral formats.
- After formats were proven, the campaigns were distributed to tens of thousands of creators across Instagram, TikTok and YouTube.
- Alex recommends running all three platforms from the start. Each has a different audience and algorithm, so one budget gives compounding reach and shows quickly where the format performs best.

chunks.heading: The content formula: the content is the hook, the app is the payoff
chunks.text:
The content needs no production budget, studio or spokesperson. The recipe:
- Take trending social content (slideshows and videos).
- Use mostly stock images and videos from Pinterest and stock video sites.
- Alter them with AI so they look more original.
- Add a text overlay, then show the app.
- Always show the app through a video or picture overlay.
- Always use trending sounds. Alex says people underrate this and "it helps a lot."

Why it works, in his words:
- People watch the content, not an ad.
- The algorithm doesn't suppress it because it doesn't look like an ad.
- The product is seen by every viewer without a "sponsored" label.
- Rule of thumb: "if your app is the entire video, nobody watches. if it shows up as the punchline to something people were already engaged with, it converts without ever feeling like an ad."

chunks.heading: The cap mechanic: why blended CPM keeps falling
chunks.text:
Alex's central economics argument is that a per-post payout cap turns viral outliers into free reach.

- **Base rate:** The campaign CPM was $0.32 per 1k views (an average of $0.31-0.32 overall).
- **Benchmarks:** He says Meta averages $8-14 per 1k views, and organic influencer deals rarely go below $2 CPM once fees and flopped posts are counted.
- **Cap:** Each post had a payout range of $500 to $600.
- **Break-even:** At $0.32 CPM a creator hits the $600 max at about 1.875M views. The brand pays nothing for views beyond that.

Top clips:

| Clip | Views | Payout | Effective CPM |
|---|---|---|---|
| #1 | 53,317,845 | $500 | $0.009 per 1k |
| #2 | 18,281,051 | $600 | $0.033 per 1k |
| #3 | 13,311,281 | $600 | n/a |

- Across all 596M views and $162,805, the blended CPM landed at $0.31 and was still dropping.
- One campaign produced 450M views on only $100k of spend.
- His summary: "the bigger the campaign gets, the cheaper every view becomes."
- Takeaway: set the max payout high enough to motivate creators, and treat every clip that blows past the cap as free reach, which is "where the real ROI compounds."

chunks.heading: The creator operating system behind 24,000 consistent clips
chunks.text:
Alex says finding a format is easy compared with getting thousands of creators to execute it consistently. This brand's brief included the following, which he says separated it from about 90% of campaigns on Content Rewards:

- **Creator agreement and confidentiality upfront.** Every creator signed before seeing materials. It filters out low-effort creators and protects the format from competitors. "most brands skip this entirely. it's a costly mistake."
- **Module-by-module onboarding.** Not a PDF: a full video playbook covering account creation, warm-up, production workflow, account management rules, dos and don'ts, and payment info. It keeps quality consistent at 24,000 clips.
- **Weekly-updated content bank.** A library of angles, hooks, prompts and templates, so creators see the newest viral formats. "the brief tells creators what to make. the content bank makes it frictionless to actually make it."
- **Influencer version of the app.** A website where creators could build personalized overlays and videos of the app and download them for their content. Alex calls this probably the biggest differentiator from other app campaigns.
- **AI content training.** Videos teaching creators to use AI for app content, plus a prompt bank.
- **Account warm-up targeting.** Creators consumed content from the brand's exact demographic before posting, so the algorithm learned who the account was for and showed clips to the right audience.
- **Leaderboard bonus on top of CPM.** Top creators were rewarded by actual app downloads via link-in-bio. Alex's logic: "views are great. installs are better." It created a second incentive layer driving reach and conversion at once.

His rule: "treat creator onboarding like a product." The brief is the bare minimum; the system produces consistent clips.

chunks.heading: Scaling timeline
chunks.text:
- **January-February:** Small test campaigns with $1k-$5k budgets, validating which formats translated into the Content Rewards ecosystem.
- **March:** First large campaigns went live and momentum built.
- **April:** The spike month. Peak days hit 28M views in 24 hours, and "the system is fully locked in."
- **May:** Sustained 15-22M views per day and still running.
- **Why margins held:** As an app there is no inventory or fulfillment, so the margin on the $700k looks nothing like a traditional business.
- **His closing claim:** "running campaigns on Content Rewards in 2026 is like running Facebook ads in 2018."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex's case study of an app that scaled to $200k MRR with 651M views and $173K in creator payouts using seven clipping campaigns. Covers finding a format first, running parallel campaigns, writing briefs that hook viewers, using payout caps for free reach, and building a small dedicated creator base.

chunks.heading: Starting from a proven format before scaling a campaign
chunks.text:
Alex says founders make a common mistake: they launch a clipping campaign before they have a working format. The app in this case study already had a great product and a tested winning format, and scaled by amplifying it with clippers.

- "You can't skip this."
- Clippers need an idea of which formats will do well and which won't.
- Scaling something that already works is what let the campaign "go crazy".
- Alex's rule: "find your format before you scale it."

chunks.heading: The case study results: 651M views for $0.27 effective CPM
chunks.text:
An app on Content Rewards scaled to $200k MRR in 3 months. Alex gives these numbers:

- 651 million views generated.
- $173K paid out to creators ($173,365 spent in total).
- Over $1,000,000 generated in the last 90 days.
- Effective CPM of $0.27 across all seven campaigns.
- For comparison, Meta charges $8-14 per thousand impressions.

He argues "no other marketing technique will ever generate a result as good as this". He says many app founders still run Meta at very high CPMs or pay influencers flat fees and get poor results.

chunks.heading: Running several campaigns at once to learn faster
chunks.text:
The app ran seven campaigns instead of opening one and hoping it pops off.

- Each campaign had different rates, caps and formats. Some paid a $1 CPM and some a $0.50 CPM.
- Each campaign tested a different variable.
- Running them together showed which formats worked in weeks instead of months.
- The biggest campaign did $77,225 in payouts and 187.5 million views.
- The smallest did $1,546 in payouts.
- Both were useful: the winner showed what to scale, the flop showed what to stop doing.

Alex's rule: run multiple campaigns at the same time and change certain settings in each, so you learn what does best while spending.

chunks.heading: How the brief changed approval rate and CPM
chunks.text:
The first campaign brief was "$1 per 1,000 views to make videos about the app". It had no strict rules. It generated 212 million views with an 89.9% approval rate.

A later brief was "submit any video where you talk about a TikTok feature, then mention the app at the end".

- It had the highest approval rate of all campaigns, 98.7%.
- It pulled 169.2M views with a very strong engagement rate.
- It ran at a $0.50 CPM, half the earlier campaign's rate.

Alex's explanation: a video that starts with something interesting pulls the viewer in and keeps them watching to the end. A video that opens with the product is more boring and tends to generate fewer views and conversions. His takeaway is to ask creators to mention your app at the end.

chunks.heading: Small groups of serious creators beat large groups of casual ones
chunks.text:
Alex says big campaigns don't necessarily have thousands of posters.

- The campaign with 169 million views had only 33 creators.
- The campaign with 67.3M views had only 42 creators.
- One creator posted 366 times and earned $12,084. Another posted 387 times.

He concludes that "a small group of serious creators is SO much better than a big group of less serious ones".

chunks.heading: Building dedicated creators instead of renting them
chunks.text:
Alex says creators who work nonstop and make consistently high-quality content tend to be loyal to the platform they already work for, so you have to make your own. His three-part approach:

1. **Make a very thorough course.** Guide creators from A to Z and teach everything you know about clipping and what works for your product.
2. **Host regular live calls.** Teach, do page reviews and bring in a guest speaker if you can. The more valuable the calls, the more creators learn.
3. **Run private 1-1 mentoring.** Set up a Discord server and hire mentors who know what they're doing. Select 100-200 clippers and have coaches guide them until they're experts.

chunks.heading: Payout caps turn viral reach into free distribution
chunks.text:
Alex treats the payout cap as a main lever on return.

- On a $1 CPM with a $500 cap, a creator is capped at 500K views. Everything past that costs nothing.
- He says this gets "insanely effective once your campaign goes big".
- The carousel campaign paid out $15,151 for 67.3M views, an effective CPM of $0.22.
- The story format campaign paid out $33,751 for 169.2M views, an effective CPM of about $0.199.
- Across all seven campaigns the final CPM was $0.27.

His rule: set a good cap, because every view past it is free reach and a decent cap gives a very good ROI.

chunks.heading: Tightening campaign settings with each round
chunks.text:
The campaigns improved as the team learned, and they spent "wayy better" than before.

- Minimum views per post (MVR) went from 300 in the first campaign to 500 in the next.
- The first few campaigns had no submission cap. Towards the end they capped it at 5 per user.
- Approval rates rose from 89.9% to 95.3% to 96.5% to 98.7% from first to last campaign.
- Each campaign taught them how to set MVR, the best cap and which formats work.

Alex's rule: keep adjusting the MVR, the cap and other settings as you go.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex lays out a 90-day plan to go from nothing to $10k+/mo as a content clipper, who reposts brand footage for pay per view. It covers niche and campaign selection, dedicated accounts, a daily batch editing workflow built around hooks, how earnings compound with account history, and hiring editors for leverage.

chunks.heading: Choosing campaigns by niche and CPM, and why Alex starts with high CPM
chunks.text:
Alex's pick for zero money, zero followers, zero reputation is content clipping. He spent 2 years on dropshipping, SMMA and freelancing first, and says none of it worked from zero the way clipping does.

- Campaign selection is "the highest-leverage decision you make as a clipper", and most beginners overlook it.
- Niches he lists, in the order he'd try them:
  - Streamer clipping (Kai Cenat, Drewski, Clavicular): $0.8-$1 per 1k views.
  - Event clipping (gatherings, boxing matches, weddings): $2-$5 per 1k views.
  - Crypto (fintech, memecoins, games): $5 per 1k views.
- Day 1 plan: pick 2-3 campaigns in the highest-CPM niche available, probably crypto or fintech, maybe betting if a strong campaign is running.
- He knows people "absolutely PRINTING" on the lower-CPM campaigns, because they like the niche (streaming, comedy, entertainment) and are simply better at it.
- He would spend a few hours trying every niche until he finds what he's genuinely good at and enjoys clipping.
- Day 1 setup takes about 30 minutes: sign up on Content Rewards (about 10 minutes, connect socials, get verified) and download CapCut (free), the only tool he needs.

chunks.heading: Why clipping works: the shift away from paid ads
chunks.text:
- Brands used to put $10M, $20M, $100M+ a year into Meta, Google and YouTube ads. Alex says that model is breaking: ad costs are up 40%+ year over year, and Gen Z skips anything that looks sponsored in under a second.
- Brands instead pay regular people to post organic-looking content from their own accounts at about $0.30 CPM, which he calls 10-30x cheaper than ads. The content gets watched because it looks like a real person sharing something real.
- How it works: the brand uploads raw footage and a campaign blueprint to a platform. The clipper edits a short clip with a strong hook and posts it from their own account. The brand gets organic reach, and the clipper is paid by views.
- The clipper doesn't film, doesn't need an audience and needs no experience. The brand supplies the footage, direction and angles that work.
- A 0-follower account can get hundreds of thousands of views because short-form algorithms "care whether people watch past the first 3 seconds", not who you are.
- Pattern he has seen in hundreds of clippers (students, laid-off people, people in countries with no access to traditional job markets): a slow start, a sharp inflection around day 30-45, then compounding.

chunks.heading: Dedicated accounts per niche
chunks.text:
- Alex creates a fresh account for each niche rather than using a personal account.
- Reasoning: posting memes, personal content and clips from 3 niches on one account confuses the audience graph, so the algorithm doesn't know who to show content to and performance is inconsistent.
- Dedicated accounts give "clean signal", which means better distribution from day 1. He calls this a detail that separates serious clippers from hobbyists.

chunks.heading: Week 1: the ugly phase, and the 30-day curve
chunks.text:
- Week 1 goal is not money, it's two things: build the editing muscle and wake up the algorithm.
- Earnings might be about $10 for the whole week (he later cites about $60). Clips take too long and hooks feel awkward.
- Speed compounds with reps: clip 1 may take 20 minutes, clip 15 about 10, clip 30 under 6.
- New accounts need consistent activity before they get real distribution, so he posts 3-5 clips a day even if they're mediocre.
- Week 1 routine:
  - Pull raw footage from his 2 campaigns.
  - Study the campaign blueprints (exact direction on what to make, which hooks and angles work).
  - Watch top-performing clips in the niche on TikTok and Reels, studying hooks: "what makes you stop scrolling?"
  - Make 3-5 clips a day and post them anyway.
- He says people who fail almost always fail here, judging everything on 7 days of data, while the person who pushes through is about 3 weeks from a first real payday.
- Days 15-30: after 100+ clips he reads his Content Rewards dashboard (which hooks performed, which posts paid, which campaigns have the best CPMs) instead of guessing. Hook instinct built on real reps is "worth more than any course or guide".
- Account velocity: platforms reward accounts that show up daily. Posts 1-5 on a new account average about 800 views; posts 50+ average 23,000+, for the same quality of content.
- Earnings trajectory he projects: about $60 in week 1, $200-$600 across weeks 2-3, $1,000-$3,000 by day 30, depending on niche and volume.

chunks.heading: The batch editing workflow (days 8-14 onward)
chunks.text:
Alex calls batch editing the unlock that separates $500/mo creators from $10k+/mo creators. Total is about 2 hours a day for 10+ unique clips, and each clip works for the next 48-72 hours.

- 10 minutes: pull raw assets from active campaigns.
- 15 minutes: write 5 hook variations per campaign in a notes app before opening the editor. He calls this the most important 15 minutes of the day because "the hook determines 90% of a clip's performance".
- 60-75 minutes: edit the first clip for campaign 1, then duplicate the project, swap the hook and export. Each variation after the first takes 3-4 minutes because the body stays the same.
- 10 minutes: schedule everything.
- Posting windows: early morning (6-7am EST) and late night (9-11pm EST). He cites data across 120,000+ clips on his platform: these windows average 84k and 91k views versus 22k in the midday dead zone.
- By end of week 2 he expects 60-80 clips posted and a few clips reaching 5k-15k views.

chunks.heading: Compounding: trust score, premium campaigns and CPM stacking (days 30-60)
chunks.text:
- Trust score on Content Rewards rises with each completed campaign. Higher trust unlocks premium campaigns paying 2-3x base CPM, so the same clips earn more per view.
- CPM stacking: running 2-3 campaigns in the same niche from one account. He says it's not recommended and not allowed in most campaigns, but worth experimenting with. Logic: an account that has posted crypto for 30 days has a tuned audience graph, so a second crypto campaign benefits from that graph-building.
- By then the batch routine is locked in at 2 hours each morning, producing 12-15 clips a day that perform better than month-1 clips.
- Projected earnings at day 60: $5,000-$10,000/mo.

chunks.heading: Scaling with editors, and what clipping builds (days 60-90)
chunks.text:
- Up to day 60 earnings are tied to his own output. Around day 60-75 he'd hire 1-2 editors (local or found online), teach them his exact batch workflow, give them campaign access, review their clips and post them.
- Pay: 10-30% of the revenue their clips generate. His output doubles or triples without more of his time.
- Projected earnings at day 90 with 1-2 editors: $10,000-$20,000/mo.
- Skills built along the way: hook writing, video editing, content distribution, algorithmic understanding, direct response marketing, campaign analytics. He says these are what brands and startups are hiring for, learned while getting paid.
- Also built: connections with brands and creators, a reputation (trust score and a portfolio of executed campaigns), and real cash profit rather than revenue that goes to overhead or loans.
- Clipping can be a destination or a launchpad: start a business with the marketing skills, launch your own brand and promote it for free with clipping, build an agency, or invest. He himself started a business making this easier for brands and creators.
- His closing advice: skip the "lock in leap of faith" and just sign up, pick a campaign and make the first clip (about 20 minutes, probably won't go viral). Then make the second, the tenth and the 69th.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex pitches "content arbitrage": brands pay everyday people to clip and repost their footage on TikTok, Reels and Shorts because many organic posts look like a cultural moment rather than an ad. He gives income tiers, the three levers separating top earners (volume, niche, hooks), and urges joining early. It is also a promotion for his employer's platform, so the income claims are unverified.

chunks.heading: Content arbitrage: how paid creators replace ad spend
chunks.text:
Alex describes "content arbitrage" as the model behind Content Rewards, where he is CMO. A brand supplies raw footage, talking points and sometimes the exact hook. Everyday people re-edit it to look native to TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts and post it from their own accounts. Creators are paid per view, per post, or both.

- His pitch for brands: paid ads in 2026 are "brutal". He cites CPMs up 40% year over year, record ad fatigue, and Gen Z skipping anything that looks sponsored within half a second.
- Brands used to put $50k-$100k into Meta ads. His claim is that if 500 regular accounts post organic-looking content at once, "the algorithm doesn't see an ad campaign, it sees a cultural moment", and "moments go viral. ads don't".
- Creators need no camera, audience, face on screen or original ideas.
- He says he has processed $1.3M+ to creators in his network at age 16, and that the business has generated "billions of views for brands".

chunks.heading: Why posting the same video many times does not get flagged as spam
chunks.text:
Alex argues the same core content can be posted hundreds of times because each repost registers as unique.

- Every re-edit, even a slight one, registers as a new piece of content.
- A different account means a different audience graph, a different caption means a different text signal, and a different posting time means a different distribution window.
- So one message reaches 500 separate audience pools at once. If even 10% of the clips take off, the campaign gets millions of views.
- He says this was tested across thousands of campaigns and "the pattern holds every time".
- One clip can be repackaged 50+ ways, each version performing independently. Creators on his campaigns post 3-4 variations of the same concept in one week, and the views and payouts stack.

chunks.heading: Creator income tiers and how earnings compound
chunks.text:
He gives income tiers "based on real data from creators in our network":

- **Beginner (first 30 days):** 1-2 clips per day, about 1-2 hours of work, $50-$999/mo, while learning which hooks and edits the algorithm rewards.
- **Intermediate (60-90 days):** 3-5 clips per day across 2-3 campaigns, $1,000-$5,000/mo, with invitations to higher-paying campaigns from a good track record.
- **Advanced (6+ months, consistent):** 5+ campaigns at once, batch editing and scheduling, $8,000-$15,000/mo, with outliers at $30k-$50k/mo during peak campaign windows.

Why it compounds, in his words:
1. Editing gets faster (30 minutes drops to 8).
2. A higher trust score earns better rates from brands.
3. Creators learn which niches pay the highest CPMs.
4. A portfolio gets them into premium campaigns instantly.

His warning: the person who makes $800 in month one and quits leaves about $10k/mo on the table six months later.

chunks.heading: What separates $500/mo creators from $15k/mo creators
chunks.text:
Alex names three differences after watching thousands of people go through the model.

1. **Volume and consistency.** Top earners run it like an operation. They batch-edit 20-30 clips on a Sunday, schedule them across the week and let the system run, rather than posting when inspired.
2. **Niche selection.** Crypto, fintech and betting campaigns pay 3-5x more per view than lifestyle or fashion. The best earners pick 2-3 high-CPM verticals and go deep.
3. **Hook engineering.** The first 1-2 seconds decide the outcome. Top creators test 5+ hooks on the same clip. In his example, one version got 2k views and another with a different opening overlay got 800k. He calls it "pattern recognition, not talent", and says it takes 2-3 weeks of testing to develop.

chunks.heading: Removing friction with platform infrastructure
chunks.text:
Alex argues the old barrier was friction, not skill: cold-DMing brands, negotiating rates on each deal, chasing invoices for weeks, and hoping to get paid.

- The platform flow he describes: sign up, browse campaigns from verified brands, pick ones that match your style, follow the blueprint (what to post and how), post from your own accounts, watch the balance update in real time, and request payout weekly via PayPal, crypto or bank transfer.
- "No invoicing. no contracts. no chasing."
- He says this shift took the model from niche to mainstream in 12 months.
- His own start: about two years earlier he was spam-DMing people on TikTok, begging them to clip videos for free, with no connections or money.

chunks.heading: Timing: why the supply gap is the opportunity
chunks.text:
He argues demand for organic creator content is growing much faster than the supply of creators.

- Some campaigns are currently struggling to fill creator slots, so acceptance rates are high, per-view payouts are generous and competition is low.
- He predicts that as more people join, payouts compress and acceptance becomes selective. Six months out, "the barrier will be higher and the per-clip earnings will be lower".
- Early creators who build reputation and trust scores now get locked into premium campaigns before the next wave is verified.
- He frames it as non-zero-sum: more creators means more brands sign up, which means more money. He cites a creator economy "set to hit $480 billion by 2027".
- His call to action is to sign up, get verified, pick a first campaign and post a first clip the same day. The only requirements he lists are a phone, a few hours a week and willingness to start.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex argues paid ads are structurally losing to volume-based organic creator distribution. Brands give raw footage and blueprints to hundreds or thousands of ordinary creators who post native-looking clips, which the algorithm treats as a trend. Includes his claimed CTR/CPM numbers and how the skill compounds. Note: promotes his own platform, Content Rewards, and the figures are self-reported.

chunks.heading: Why Alex says paid ads are structurally losing to organic creator content
chunks.text:
- Alex argues people no longer trust branded content: an ad is filed in the brain as "someone trying to take my money," while a regular person talking about a product from their bedroom "feels like a recommendation from a peer."
- Meta ad costs are up 40%+ year over year, attention spans are shorter, and people skip anything that looks sponsored.
- His measured numbers across hundreds of campaigns: branded paid ads average 1.2% CTR, organic creator clips average 5.8% CTR, which he calls "4x the conversion."
- Organic clips cost 10-30x less to distribute, so a brand gets more trust and more reach for a fraction of the price.
- He claims platforms are getting better at suppressing paid content and promoting organic, so the gap widens every quarter.
- Context he gives: he is 16 and runs Virality, an agency that has coordinated 100,000+ creators and generated billions of organic views for brands.

chunks.heading: The volume model: hundreds of imperfect clips instead of one perfect ad
chunks.text:
- Alex's core mechanic: a brand moves its marketing budget from Meta to hundreds or thousands of regular people.
- Each person gets the brand's raw footage, talking points and guidelines, edits it into a short clip, and posts it from their own account.
- Each clip looks native because a real person chose to post it.
- When around 500 accounts post about the same product in the same week, "the algorithm doesn't register a marketing campaign. it registers a trend," and pushes the content to millions for free.
- Everyone in the chain wins: the brand gets reach, creators get paid, the platform gets content volume, viewers get entertainment instead of ads.
- His framing: "the company spending $10M on ads is fighting the algorithm. the company paying 1,000 creators $3k each is riding it. same total spend. completely different results."
- Because every creator edits differently, content constantly refreshes, which avoids the 2-3 week creative fatigue of paid ads.

chunks.heading: Economics: a $10M ad department vs a creator network
chunks.text:
Alex's side-by-side comparison:

| | $10M/year ad operation | Organic creator network |
|---|---|---|
| Team | 15-30 person marketing team, $800k+/year salaries | 500-10,000 creators with phones |
| CPM | $10-$50 | $0.20-$0.50 |
| Average CTR | 1.2% | 4.8% |
| Impressions | ~1.4 billion/year | comparable or greater |
| Creative | fatigues after 2-3 weeks | refreshes constantly |
| Total cost | full budget | 3%-10% of the ad budget |

- Note he cites 5.8% CTR for organic in one place and 4.8% in this comparison; treat the organic figure as roughly 5%.
- His takeaway: a single creator posting 5-10 clips a day from a phone generates more engaged reach per dollar than the whole ad department, because "the system you're plugged into is structurally superior."

chunks.heading: How short-form distribution actually works (why a new account can win)
chunks.text:
- Clip performance depends on the quality of the hook and the algorithm's response to early engagement, "not based on your follower count. not based on your production quality."
- A brand new account with 0 followers can outperform a branded 100k-follower account if the opening 3 seconds are better.
- Short-form algorithms distribute on engagement signals, not status, so the barrier to entry is not money, equipment or connections.
- The craft is repackaging raw brand footage with a strong hook, clean editing and the right pacing for the platform. He says most people use CapCut (free) and need about 2 weeks of practice to make a solid 20-second clip.
- Editing takes 5-8 minutes per clip once the workflow is down.

chunks.heading: The compounding effects of consistent posting
chunks.text:
Alex lists four things that compound with volume:

- **Editing speed:** clip 1 takes 25 minutes, clip 50 takes 5 minutes, clip 200 takes 3 minutes.
- **Hook instinct:** after testing hundreds of hooks you develop near-subconscious pattern recognition. He calls this "the single highest-leverage skill in marketing and it only comes from volume."
- **Algorithmic trust:** accounts that post daily get preferential distribution, and the algorithm gives bigger test audiences the more you feed it.
- **Platform trust:** on Content Rewards, each completed campaign raises a trust score, and a higher score unlocks premium campaigns paying 2-3x the base rate.
- His illustrative earnings path: about $500 in month 1, and $5,000-$8,000 in month 4 for the same 2-hour daily routine.
- His rule of thumb: somewhere around clip 15-20, speed picks up, hooks sharpen and the algorithm starts trusting the content.

chunks.heading: Timing: the supply/demand window in creator marketing
chunks.text:
- Alex says the organic creator model is still early: brands are joining faster than creators, and some Content Rewards campaigns can't fill their creator slots.
- Consequences he lists: easy acceptance with no track record, generous CPMs because brands compete for creators, and low competition per campaign.
- He cites creator signups growing 40% month over month and expects payouts to tighten and the balance to shift within 6-8 months.
- He compares it to earlier windows (YouTube AdSense, Amazon FBA, UGC creation), where early movers made the most before margins compressed.
- His claim: "the window is obvious in hindsight but invisible to most people while it's open." He also says organic will always stay more affordable and accessible than ads.
- Note: Alex is CMO of Content Rewards, the platform he recommends, so this section is also promotion for it.

chunks.heading: Alex's step-by-step start for a new creator
chunks.text:
1. Sign up on Content Rewards and get verified.
2. Browse campaigns by category and pick one in an interesting niche or one that pays well, ideally both.
3. Download the brand's raw assets and read the campaign blueprint (angles, hooks, look and feel).
4. Open CapCut and make a first clip. He expects it to take about 20 minutes and probably not go viral.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex argues Netflix wastes $2.9B on marketing ($89 per subscriber) while suppressing its cheapest channel, user clips. Using Kick's clipping program as proof, he lays out a tiered CPM-paid clipper model that could cut CAC to $1.2-$4, and why incumbents won't adopt it.

chunks.heading: Netflix's $89 cost per subscriber vs. a clipper program
chunks.text:
- Alex's headline claim: Netflix spent $2.9 billion on marketing in 2024, including $1.7 billion in pure advertising (billboards, YouTube pre-roll, Facebook ads, the Super Bowl spot). It added roughly 32 million subscribers.
- That works out to $89 per subscriber, and "over $100" in some estimates for the US market.
- His thesis is that Netflix pays 14x more than it should, while "actively destroying their cheapest growth channel".
- The contrast case is Kick, a Twitch competitor backed by Stake. In September 2024 its clipping program generated over 30 billion views in one month, for roughly $6 million at a $0.2 CPM.
- Alex says Netflix's marketing budget could fund 40 programs that size.

chunks.heading: Why clips work: "commercials that don't feel like commercials"
chunks.text:
- Alex's reading of Kick: "clips are commercials that don't feel like commercials."
- A 45-second clip of a streamer's best moment doesn't read as an ad. The viewer thinks "I need to see more of this", so the clip creates desire for the full content.
- Streamers on Kick don't need to grow their own TikTok presence, because the clipping program extracts, edits and distributes their best moments to people who have never heard of Kick.
- Alex's rule of thumb: "Every clip is a commercial. It just doesn't feel like one."

chunks.heading: The math for a Netflix clipper program
chunks.text:
Alex's conservative assumptions:
- Pay clippers $0.6 per thousand views (higher than Kick, to attract quality).
- 10 billion views a month (less than Kick's 30 billion).
- Only 0.05% of viewers convert to subscribers.

Result:
- $6 million monthly spend, 5 million new subscribers a month, $1.2 per subscriber.
- That is a ~74% improvement over $89, by his own framing.
- Sensitivity check: even if his conversion rate is 10x too optimistic, cost per subscriber is $12, still far below $89.
- This ignores the added brand awareness, social proof and content discovery from Netflix clips being everywhere.

chunks.heading: The distribution problem: content nobody discovers
chunks.text:
- Netflix has 7,500 titles in its US library and releases 13-14 new originals every week. Alex says most people have heard of maybe 30 of them.
- His diagnosis: "This isn't a content problem." It's a distribution problem.
- Netflix's recommendation algorithm only works on people who already subscribe. Discovery before subscribing happens on TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts, where he cites 500 million people.
- His view is that Netflix sits on 7,500 potential viral moments and pays lawyers to make sure nobody sees them.
- What Netflix does today when someone posts a 45-second clip: a DMCA takedown and a strike on the creator's account. The creator moves on to platforms that don't attack them, the show loses organic discovery, viewership disappoints, and it is cancelled after one season.
- Example he uses: the Wednesday dance scene hit 1.5 billion views across platforms and drove major subscriber growth. Netflix paid nothing for it. Alex says it happened "despite their content protection strategy, not because of any distribution effort."
- The alternative: 10,000 clippers actively hunting moments across the whole library, paid to find and distribute the best scenes.

chunks.heading: Program structure Alex would build (three tiers)
chunks.text:
Alex says he has built networks with 100,000+ creators, and lays out this structure:
- **Tier 1, open program:** anyone can join. $0.6 CPM. Clips must be 15-60 seconds with a "watch on netflix" watermark. Paid weekly.
- **Tier 2, verified partners:** creators with a 1 million view minimum. $1 CPM. Early access to new releases and dedicated support.
- **Tier 3, exclusive creators:** the top 50 performers. $2 CPM plus bonuses, premiere event access, and revenue share on attributable conversions.

Projected economics:
- Annual cost: $72 to $200 million.
- New subscribers: 26 to 60 million.
- Cost per subscriber: $1.2 to $4, which he calls "ATLEAST 32x better" than $89.
- The spend is less than 7% of Netflix's current marketing budget.

chunks.heading: Why incumbents won't do it
chunks.text:
Alex lists five organizational reasons, none about whether it would work:
1. The legal team has too much power, and the content-protection infrastructure would have to reverse. "People don't dismantle their own departments."
2. It means admitting the current strategy was wrong, which is hard to tell a board after billions of traditional spend.
3. Attribution is messy. You can't pixel-track someone who saw a TikTok clip and subscribed three weeks later, and marketing teams hate what they can't measure perfectly.
4. It feels like giving content away, even though a 45-second clip of a two-hour movie gives away nothing and creates demand.
5. Someone's job depends on DMCA enforcement, and that person will fight it.

chunks.heading: Prediction: how the shift happens
chunks.text:
- Alex expects a "hungry number two or three player" to figure it out, not Netflix or Disney, because they are too big and set in their ways.
- When that player launches a serious clipper program and sees subscriber growth that doesn't match its other spend, everyone will notice and copy it.
- He points to the same pattern at Netflix: ad-supported tiers, password-sharing crackdowns, live sports. The playbook is "resist the obvious move, watch a competitor prove it works, copy it two years later, pretend it was the plan all along."
- His positioning: his company (Content Rewards) already has the infrastructure, with 100,000+ creators, automatic creator payouts and quality control systems, so it will be ready when other companies "figure out what Kick already knows."

this campaign had a vault of slideshow formats, a prompt bank, a Gemini tutorial and live calls

a new creator could join and understand what to make without spending 3 days asking questions

your brief should show a complete example: the opening slide, how the story develops, where the app comes in and what the viewer should do next

then explain what they can change

otherwise you get people copying the same post word for word, or making something completely unrelated to why anyone would download your app

139 creators submitted content here.

60 had at least one post approved.

10 generated 21m of the 23.1m views.

you don't know who those 10 are when you launch.

that's why you need to test different creators. but once someone starts working, actually pay attention to them

give them feedback, help them develop more angles, and make sure they have enough material to keep going

keep recruiting too. you want more people like them, not a campaign that depends on one person being available.

the top creator posted 324 times and generated 6.2m views.

when something works, figure out what you can repeat.

was it the opening line? the situation people recognised? how the product was introduced?

keep that part and test a different story around it

if you change everything, you learn nothing. if you repost the exact same thing forever, you eventually run out of road

-> fund it in stages

they started with $4k and topped up over four months to eventually reach $21k

start with an amount you can afford to test, and use it to find promising creators and formats before increasing the budget
